newsYesterday.headline: Stock Rotation Hits AI Winners on Spending Worries: Markets Wrap

simpleYesterday.bigPicture: Big Tech had a bad day. Alphabet (Google) lost a record $500bn in value after saying its new AI search mode is eating into its old search business, and Amazon and Intel fell after hours. Investors moved money out of tech and into government bonds, so US borrowing costs fell — the 10-year yield dropped back below 5%. That happened even though the economy grew faster than expected (3.4%) and inflation rose to 3.6%, and markets still expect the Fed to raise rates in December. In Europe stocks rose, the ECB held rates and Christine Lagarde said she will step down early. Oil stayed above $100 as the US weighs new strikes on Iran after next week’s elections.

forces.title: Why Alphabet’s Fall Shook the Whole Market
forces.analogy: Like a star chef admitting the new menu is stealing customers from the old one — diners wonder whether all the money spent on the new kitchen will pay off.
forces.explanation: Alphabet’s search revenue grew 12% to $63.4bn, missing estimates, and Google admitted its “AI mode” answers are eating into traditional search ads. It also burned $9.1bn of cash as AI capex hit $51.3bn in the quarter. The shares fell about 13%, wiping out roughly $500bn — a record for Alphabet and the second-biggest one-day loss in Wall Street history.
forces.source: Financial Times — “Alphabet shares tumble in $500bn rout” (Oct 29, 2026)
forces.whyItMatters: If AI starts eating the profits of existing businesses before it earns its own, investors may demand less spending — bad news for chipmakers and data-centre builders.

forces.title: Why Yields Fell Even With a Strong Economy
forces.analogy: Like people running into a shop to get out of the rain — they’re not there because the shop is great, they just want shelter.
forces.explanation: The economy grew at a 3.4% pace in Q3 and PCE inflation rose to 3.6%, which would normally push yields up. But when tech stocks fell, investors bought government bonds for safety, and a lower oil price helped too (FT), pushing the 10-year yield down to about 4.93%.
forces.source: Financial Times — “US economy beats forecasts to grow at 3.4% rate”; “US tech stocks fall after earnings fuel AI spending concerns” (Oct 29, 2026)
forces.whyItMatters: Lower yields make borrowing cheaper, but with an 83.5% chance of a December hike priced in, a fear-driven bond rally can reverse quickly.

forces.title: Why Oil Stays Above $100
forces.analogy: Like a forecast of a storm next week — nothing has happened yet, but people still stock up.
forces.explanation: The WSJ reported that the US told Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense military campaign against Iran after the Nov 3 midterms, and the FT reports Israel’s inconclusive election leaves Netanyahu free to join one. At the same time there is new diplomacy, so prices are high but not rising every day.
forces.source: FT — “European gas prices jump above €100…” (Oct 28) and “Israel vote leaves door open to Iran attack” (Oct 29); The National (Oct 28)
forces.whyItMatters: Expensive oil keeps inflation high, which is one reason the Fed may still raise rates in December.

library.title: Markets trade the surprise, not the level
library.text: Investors already expect a number (the consensus). Prices move on the gap between the actual and that expectation.

library.title: Two channels: cash flows and the discount rate
library.text: Every headline reaches prices through expected profits, the discount rate, or both. A strong jobs report can lift profits and yields at the same time: the net effect decides.

library.title: Good news can be bad news
library.text: When inflation is the main worry, strong data raises the odds of higher rates, and stocks can fall on it.

library.title: In a cap-weighted index, the giants decide
library.text: A handful of mega-caps make up a large share of the S&P 500. The index can fall on a day when most of its stocks rise, and the reverse.

library.title: The Dow is price-weighted
library.text: The Dow weights companies by share price, not size. A few high-priced stocks can push it the other way from the S&P 500.

library.title: Growth stocks behave like long bonds
library.text: Most of a growth company's value sits in profits far in the future. When rates or confidence change, those distant cash flows swing the most.

library.title: One company's revenue is another's cost
library.text: The AI build-out helps the sellers of chips and memory and squeezes the buyers. 'Tech' is not one block.

library.title: Markets hate uncertainty more than bad news
library.text: Fear spikes when the outcome is unknown; once it is known, volatility often fades even if the news is bad.

library.title: Flight to quality
library.text: In a scare, money leaves risky assets for safe ones: Treasuries rally (yields fall), and the dollar, yen, Swiss franc and gold tend to firm.

library.title: Supply shocks are the hardest case
library.text: An oil shock pushes inflation up and growth down at the same time, leaving central banks with no good option.

library.title: Look at real rates
library.text: Policy is only tight if the rate is well above inflation. Rate minus inflation tells you how restrictive the central bank really is.

library.title: Results versus expectations, and guidance
library.text: A company can beat estimates and still fall if the outlook disappoints: prices follow the future, not last quarter.

library.title: Short term: headlines. Long term: profits
library.text: Over days, prices move on fear and news. Over years, they follow earnings.

library.title: Read the curve, not only the level
library.text: If the 2-year moves most, the market is changing its view on the central bank. If the 30-year moves most, it is about inflation, growth or fiscal risk.

trumpImpact.weeklySummary: The final week before the midterms was dominated by Iran and the Fed. NPR reported on Oct 22 that the US and Israel were preparing for a possible attack on Iran in early November, after the US vote. Trump said on Oct 25 he had a “decision to make”, and on Oct 28 the Wall Street Journal reported that Washington had told Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense campaign after Nov 3. Israel’s inconclusive Oct 27 election leaves Netanyahu free to join such a campaign as caretaker prime minister (FT). Mediators kept talking: Qatar gave Iran a new draft deal and the WSJ reported US outreach to Tehran. Oil stayed above $100 and European gas topped €100/MWh. On Oct 28 the Fed held rates in a split vote; Trump spared his own appointee, Chair Warsh, but blamed the committee, and Warsh said politics played no role. Meanwhile Bloomberg reported that the AI industry’s bet on Trump is running into a new political reality, and candidates of both parties are calling for action on AI data centres (Yahoo Finance).

majorMoves.title: US Signals Possible Renewed Strikes on Iran After the Midterms
majorMoves.background: NPR reported on Oct 22 that the US and Israel were preparing for a possible attack on Iran in early November, after the midterms, and that the US was amassing forces in the region. On Oct 25 Trump said he had a “decision to make”, and on Oct 28 the WSJ reported that Washington had told several Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense campaign after Nov 3 (via FT and The National). The FT reported on Oct 29 that Israel’s inconclusive election leaves Netanyahu free to launch fresh strikes with the US as caretaker PM. Houthi rebels kept firing at Saudi targets, including a missile at Taif. At the same time Qatar gave Iran a new draft deal, Trump told Axios talks were happening through mediators, and the WSJ reported Vice President Vance had reached out to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s top security body.

impact.equities: European oil majors raised payouts: Shell lifted its quarterly buyback to $5bn and TotalEnergies beat forecasts (FT). ExxonMobil’s CEO pulled out of next week’s Adipec conference in Abu Dhabi over security concerns (FT).
impact.bonds: No clear direct effect — US yields were driven by the Fed and the tech sell-off this week.
impact.commodities: WTI rose almost 3% to $102.78 on Oct 28 and front-month Brent closed near $115 (Yahoo Finance). Dutch gas jumped to €100.95/MWh, the first time above €100 since December 2022 (FT). UBS expects Brent near $110 to year-end (The National).
impact.crypto: Bitcoin fell 2.2% on the week to $79,524 (watchlist).
impact.defense: No clear lift for US defence stocks, which remain weighed down by bets on a Democratic win (see below).

majorMoves.why: Oil prices include a “risk premium” for supply that might be lost. A credible threat of renewed war in the Gulf — even with talks going on — makes buyers pay more now in case supply is cut later.

source.name: FT — “European gas prices jump above €100…” (Oct 28), “Israel vote leaves door open to Iran attack” (Oct 29); NPR (Oct 22); The National (Oct 28)

majorMoves.title: Fed Holds in a Split Vote; Trump Blames the Committee, Spares Warsh
majorMoves.background: The Fed kept rates at 3.75–4.00% after its September hike. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wanted a quarter-point rise. The Fed said the economy is “expanding at a strong pace” and will vote on rates only seven times in 2027. Warsh declined to respond to Trump’s criticism of the board and said “politics played no role” (FT). Trump has argued that rate policy hurts the economy more than inflation and accused the committee of acting out of spite, while sparing Warsh, his own appointee (Yahoo Finance).

impact.equities: Stocks edged up on the day (S&P 500 +0.28%) but fell the next day as tech sold off.
impact.bonds: The 10-year closed at 5.05% on Oct 28 (Treasury) while two-year yields eased after Warsh, then the 10-year fell to about 4.93% on Oct 29 as investors fled tech. December hike odds rose to 83.5% from 72.8% after the meeting (CME FedWatch via Investing.com).

majorMoves.why: When the Fed gives no guidance, every data release matters more, so bond prices can swing more (Bloomberg). A president publicly attacking the Fed adds to uncertainty about whether policy will stay independent.

source.name: Financial Times — Federal Reserve decision as it happened (Oct 28); Yahoo Finance (Oct 28)

majorMoves.title: Final Week Before the Midterms: AI, Diesel and Energy Deals
majorMoves.background: Democrats are strongly favoured to win the House, and candidates of both parties are calling for action on drug prices, housing and AI data centres (Yahoo Finance). Bloomberg reported that the AI industry’s bet on Trump is crashing into a new political reality (headline). New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill called Trump’s diesel deal with Putin “corrupt and illegal” and is weighing ways to block three tankers due to arrive just after the midterms, two of them under sanctions (FT). Hungary and the US signed a “Trump Peace Pipeline Framework” (Bloomberg headline).

impact.equities: AI leaders fell as the political mood toward big tech and data centres soured; Alphabet lost a record $500bn on Oct 29 (Bloomberg, FT), though mainly on its results.
impact.commodities: A block on Russian diesel cargoes would tighten US East Coast fuel supply; no confirmed price effect yet.
impact.defense: Defence stocks remain weighed down by bets that a Democratic Congress would scrap Trump’s proposed spending boost (FT, Oct 19).

majorMoves.why: Markets price policy changes before they happen. A split Congress makes big new spending or tariff laws less likely, but both parties now target AI data centres and drug prices — sectors that have led the market.

forwardLook.text: Democrats are favoured to win the House; the Senate is less clear (Yahoo Finance). Tariffs, defence, drug prices and AI data centres are the market-sensitive issues.

forwardLook.title: Possible renewed strikes on Iran
forwardLook.text: The WSJ reported the US told Gulf states to prepare for a short, intense campaign after the vote, and Israel’s caretaker government could join it (FT). Talks through Qatar continue. The biggest single risk for oil and gas.

forwardLook.title: October jobs report
forwardLook.text: A strong number would firm up the 83.5% priced chance of a December hike, which Trump opposes.

forwardLook.title: Russia–Ukraine–US talks; possible Trump–Putin–Xi summit
forwardLook.text: Kremlin aide Ushakov said Witkoff and Putin discussed resuming trilateral talks in mid-November and a leaders’ summit at the Apec forum in Shenzhen (via FT, Oct 21). A local humanitarian ceasefire began around Oleshky on Oct 27 (FT).

forwardLook.title: Russian diesel cargoes
forwardLook.text: Three tankers carrying about 140,000 tonnes of Russian diesel are due at US ports just after the midterms; New Jersey’s governor is weighing ways to block them (FT).

scenarios.label: De-escalation
scenarios.text: A deal through Qatari mediators or a clear decision against new strikes pulls oil back toward $100, easing inflation fears and the case for a December hike.

scenarios.label: Escalation
scenarios.text: Renewed US strikes on Iran after Nov 3 push oil sharply higher, lift inflation expectations and make a December hike more likely.

scenarios.label: Midterm shift
scenarios.text: A Democratic House puts Trump’s defence boost and tariffs in doubt and adds scrutiny of AI data centres and drug prices — mixed for big tech and health care, negative for defence.
